This person is a 42-year-old former North Sea oil rig electrician from Aberdeen who supports net zero only if the implementation includes a legally backed Just Transition Deal: fully funded retraining vouchers tied to high-wage offshore wind and CCUS jobs in the same region, local content requirements in CfD rounds, and wage bridges so he can pay his mortgage while reskilling. After being laid off in a 2022 decommissioning, he emptied his savings to pay for a GWO course, so wage-bridging during retraining is his red line. Without a wage bridge covering at least 70% of his old £55k offshore pay, he'd have to sell his Aberdeen flat to keep up the mortgage during a year of retraining. After paying for his GWO, he was still turned down by an offshore wind contractor for lacking six months of rope-access hours he couldn’t afford to build up without an income. He wants CfD awards to require paid trainee slots that count toward rope-access hours, instead of unpaid “experience” he can’t afford.

This person is a 38-year-old HM Treasury economist in London who argues for a technology-neutral implementation: a steadily rising, economy-wide carbon price with border adjustments and a household dividend, competitive auctions without local content rules, and sunset clauses on subsidies to avoid locking in inefficient spending. Having helped review CfD auction rounds at HMT, I’ve seen tech-neutral competition slash costs, so I oppose local-content mandates. As a private renter in a draughty London flat, I want the household dividend to visibly offset higher heating costs from a rising carbon price. After my landlord declined both a heat‑pump trial and basic insulation, I realized renters like me need a visible household dividend to offset higher gas bills from a rising carbon price. Because my flat's gas account is in my landlord's name, I want the dividend paid per person via HMRC rather than through energy bills so renters like me actually receive it.

This person is a 29-year-old low-income private renter in Manchester, a single mother, who wants implementation to mandate minimum EPC C for rentals by 2028, offer landlord-targeted grants contingent on rent-freeze clauses, and require heat pump–ready wiring so her bills drop without her being priced out. Last winter her son's asthma worsened in their cold, damp EPC E flat while she paid £200 a month on a prepay meter. Her flat’s old wiring trips if she runs the kettle and the heaters together, so she wants net-zero rules to require heat pump–ready electrics in rentals. She backs grants only with rent-freeze conditions because her landlord has already hinted the rent will go up after any improvements. If upgrades aren’t tied to a rent freeze, I’ll be priced out of my area and lose the childcare help from my mum and neighbours.

This person is a 62-year-old small buy-to-let landlord in Leeds who accepts efficiency upgrades but demands phased EPC deadlines by property type, 100% capital allowances for insulation and heat pumps, low-interest green mortgages, and an appeals process for hard-to-treat terraces. After being quoted £14,000 for a heat pump that still wouldn’t get my solid‑walled terrace to EPC C, I now insist on phased deadlines and an appeals route for hard‑to‑treat homes. Two of my Victorian back‑to‑backs have long‑term tenants on modest incomes, so a single near‑term EPC C cutoff would force me to choose between steep rent rises or selling. My lender has warned my remortgage rate will jump if I can’t evidence a path to EPC C, so phased deadlines and green mortgages are make-or-break for me. Leeds planning refused external wall insulation on the street-facing wall, leaving only internal insulation that would mean weeks of disruption and temporary rehousing for my tenants.

This person is a 55-year-old Welsh upland sheep farmer near Brecon who supports net zero if agricultural methane is handled via incentives not taxes: long-term ELMs contracts with clear payment rates for peat restoration and hedgerows, grants for anaerobic digesters, and exemptions for small herds during drought years. ELMs peatland and hedgerow rates need to be fixed for 10–15 years so my bank will treat them as dependable income when renewing the farm loan. My bank manager has said he’ll only treat peat and hedgerow ELMs payments as income if the rate is fixed in the contract for at least 10 years. In the 2018 drought I sold 80 ewes just to cover feed, so a blanket methane tax without a small-herd drought exemption would have sunk us. If the hedgerow payment was locked in, I’d plant another 1.5 km along the top fields to shelter lambs and cut storm losses.

This person is a 34-year-old conservation NGO policy lead in Bristol who wants implementation to integrate climate and nature: spatial planning that prioritizes onshore wind and solar on low-biodiversity sites, mandatory biodiversity net gain for all energy projects, and redirecting ELMs toward results-based habitat outcomes with transparent monitoring. Having worked on an ELMs pilot that paid farmers for plans rather than actual habitat gains, I want results-based contracts with independent, transparent monitoring. I care most that biodiversity net gain be verified through independent, open data so developers cannot mark their own homework. After our ELMs pilot paid for ponds that were never dug, I now insist on open, independent verification linked to results-based payments. After spending months auditing a solar farm’s biodiversity net gain claims that didn’t match what was on the ground, I now insist the 2050 pathway require independent, open verification before any credits are claimed.

This person is a 45-year-old National Grid connections manager based in Reading who insists the 2050 goal requires reforms: first-ready-first-served queue management, anticipatory investment allowances from Ofgem, statutory 12-month planning timelines for new 400kV lines, and standardised curtailment rules for batteries. If Ofgem allows true anticipatory investment, I can finally build the extra 400 kV bay at Bramley ahead of need instead of waiting years for a trigger customer. I recently had to tell a 200 MW battery project near Basingstoke they’ll be waiting until 2031 because I can’t build the extra Bramley 400 kV bay without anticipatory funding. My annual KPIs and customer satisfaction scores plummet when I’m forced to issue 7–10 year dates that we could avoid with true anticipatory funding and a first‑ready‑first‑served queue. Last year I had to cancel a 400 kV breaker order for Bramley because anticipatory funding wasn’t approved.

This person is a 68-year-old parish council chair in rural Norfolk who will oppose pylons unless implementation guarantees community benefits: mandatory undergrounding near villages and heritage sites, compulsion for developers to fund local energy rebates, and enforceable construction noise limits. They still remember a year-long substation upgrade that rattled windows from 6 a.m., so they now insist on legally enforceable construction noise curfews. As a pensioner on a fixed income, they would only support the 2050 net zero goal if the required grid upgrades come with developer-funded bill rebates for local households. They live 300 metres from a proposed 400 kV pylon route, so they insist the section near the village is undergrounded. Off the gas grid and stuck with old storage heaters, developer-funded bill rebates would decide whether I can afford winter heating.

This person is a 35-year-old disabled commuter in London who backs zero-emission transport if implementation prioritizes accessibility: a national ZEBRA-style fund tied to ramp reliability metrics, retaining some curbside parking for Blue Badge users, and ring-fencing road-pricing revenue to freeze bus and Tube fares. After being stranded twice last month by broken ramps on new electric buses, I only back a ZEBRA-style fund if payouts hinge on audited ramp uptime. Last week I missed a physio session after a bus ramp failed and the lift at the next station was out of service, so tying funding to audited accessibility metrics is non-negotiable for me. As a power wheelchair user in Zone 4, if Blue Badge bays are replaced by EV chargers and fare freezes aren’t guaranteed from road-pricing revenue, I’ll be effectively cut off from work and NHS appointments. I now track every failed bus boarding and believe grants should be contingent on operators maintaining at least 99% audited ramp uptime.

This person is a 47-year-old Midlands logistics SME owner with 20 diesel vans who wants a practical phase-in: grants for electric vans and depot chargers, priority grid connections for freight depots, interoperable public chargers on motorways, and temporary exemptions or e-fuel credits in Clean Air Zones until 2030. His pilot of two electric vans collapsed after a nine-month wait for a depot grid upgrade and drivers losing hours at incompatible motorway chargers. He says the EV pilot cost him a £75,000-a-year retail delivery contract after drivers missed slots waiting at incompatible motorway chargers. Our DNO quoted £58,000 and up to a two-year wait for the 200 kVA upgrade to run six depot chargers, so without grants and a priority connection I can’t scale beyond diesel. If the policy guaranteed a six-month priority DNO connection for freight depots, I could commit to replacing five of my 20 vans by 2027.

This person is a project manager for offshore wind based in Aberdeen in his 40s who wants the UK to hit net zero by 2050 by fixing Contracts for Difference design (realistic strike prices and indexation), speeding marine planning and leasing decisions, investing in port infrastructure, and reforming the grid connection queue and offshore transmission to enable multi-purpose interconnectors, because delays have already sunk projects he worked on and threaten local jobs. After our 900 MW project collapsed when AR5’s offshore wind price cap lagged inflation, I had to let contractors go and watch planned Aberdeen port upgrades get shelved. Because AR5’s unindexed cap forced me to cancel £30m of Aberdeen SME contracts, I won’t take another project to FID without commodity-linked CfD indexation and a first-ready, first-connected grid queue. I watched our 2029 grid offer slip to 2035 because a first-come queue lets speculative projects block capacity. If AR6 indexes CfDs to steel and turbine costs, I can rebook our 2028 installation vessel and rehire my 45-person package team in Aberdeen.

This person is a Cornish inshore fisher in her 50s who supports climate action but demands that offshore wind rollout include co-designed siting to protect spawning grounds, mandatory cable burial depths and transit corridors, compensation for gear loss, and a binding community benefits fund, because she has already lost income to poorly planned marine developments. Last year, a wind survey vessel off St Ives dragged away three strings of my crab pots, costing me about £3,000 and ten days’ landings. I want a legal 2‑metre cable‑burial standard with post‑lay surveys and a no‑fault gear‑loss scheme that pays within 30 days. If cable-burial rules stay as "where practicable," my insurance won’t cover snagged gear and I carry the loss. Transit corridors need to be at least one nautical mile wide so we can steam to shelter safely in bad weather.

This person is a gas boiler engineer from Leeds in his 30s who argues the implementation should avoid cliff-edge bans and instead sequence the transition with clear, realistic phase-out dates, funded retraining, clarity on hydrogen’s role, allowance for hybrid heat pumps in hard-to-insulate homes, and robust consumer protections and warranties, because sudden rules could strand his skills and leave customers without affordable options. If hydrogen for home heating is ruled out after the village trials, I need that decision by 2026 so I can plan my qualifications and stock. I’ve put off a £4,000 heat-pump training and tooling package twice because I don’t know if I’ll be fitting hybrids, hydrogen-ready boilers, or full electrics. I’ve got two apprentices on day release at Leeds College of Building, and I need clarity now on whether to book them onto heat-pump or hydrogen courses for next term. Last winter I had to tell a pensioner in a draughty 1900s terrace in Holbeck that a full heat pump wouldn’t keep up without major insulation, which is why I want hybrids kept on the table.

This person is a retrofit coordinator and heat pump installer in Birmingham in her late 20s who wants a stable decade-long Boiler Upgrade Scheme with higher grants for social housing, heat pump–ready building regulations for all new builds from 2025, simplified MCS/PAS paperwork, and DNO-backed street-by-street upgrades so she can scale her business and cut bills for low-income clients. Two of my Birmingham cul-de-sacs waited six months for DNO sign-off, so a net zero plan with funded street-by-street upgrades would unlock dozens of installs. A decade-long, guaranteed BUS would let me hire and train two more apprentices instead of relying on short-term contracts. Last year I lost a social housing block tender because the current BUS cap left a £1,200-per-flat shortfall the landlord couldn’t cover. If the 2050 goal is backed by five-year, ring-fenced BUS funding and enforceable DNO upgrade milestones, I can commit to apprentices and kit; if it’s just a headline, I’m stuck with cancellations and cash-flow gaps.

This person is a Treasury economist in London in his 50s who supports net zero if delivered through a clear carbon pricing pathway (tightening the UK ETS cap and extending it judiciously to sectors like domestic maritime), a UK carbon border adjustment to protect industry, and revenue recycling via NIC cuts or lump-sum rebates to offset regressive impacts, because he is accountable for fiscal stability and public consent. Having spent years costing the fuel duty freeze, he now backs net zero only via predictable carbon pricing with revenues transparently recycled. Because he must defend the Red Book scorecard to the OBR, he wants a rules-based carbon price and automatic recycling, not discretionary subsidies. Having had the OBR challenge his fuel-duty assumptions, he now insists on a statutory carbon price corridor and automatic, formula-based NIC rebates to keep the Red Book scorecard neutral. After the OBR knocked billions off his forecast when fuel duty was frozen again, he now insists on a statutory carbon price corridor with automatic NIC rebates.

This person is a low-income private renter and single mother in Hull in her early 30s who wants the policy to reinstate and enforce Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards to EPC C for landlords with grant support, introduce a social energy tariff, and ban rent hikes tied to subsidy-funded upgrades, because high bills and a cold, damp home are harming her child’s health. She wants an auto-applied social energy tariff for prepay meters so she isn't paying the highest rates to keep her child warm. Last winter my son’s asthma got worse from black mould while I was topping up £10 every two days just to keep his room warm. After being switched to a prepay meter when I fell behind, I saw over £1 a day vanish in standing charges even with the heating off, so an automatic social tariff is crucial for us. When I asked for insulation, my landlord said he couldn’t afford it and threatened to raise the rent, which is why I want grants tied to a rent-rise ban.

This person is a National Grid system planner based near Warwick in his mid-40s who argues for anticipatory investment and a strategic spatial energy plan, faster consent for new high-voltage lines (targeting one-year decisions), transparent connection queue reform, and OFGEM allowances for early grid build, because decade-long lead times make 2050 targets unattainable. Last year I had to tell several shovel‑ready West Midlands projects their grid connection had slipped to the late 2030s because a 400 kV upgrade is stuck in planning, which is why I’m pushing for one‑year consents and a ready‑to‑connect queue. If net‑zero is set without consent reform and anticipatory funding, I’ll be planning for years of curtailment and constraint costs instead of new connections. Under RIIO‑2 I’m barred from building 400 kV reinforcements ahead of need even when our forecasts demand it. I strongly support moving to a first‑ready, first‑connected queue with enforceable milestones, because first‑come, first‑served is clogging my queue with speculative projects.

This person is a Somerset parish councillor and countryside campaigner in her 60s who insists that new transmission and wind projects include undergrounding in sensitive landscapes, generous community benefits and bill discounts, design codes to reduce visual impact, and meaningful consultation with route alternatives, because she has seen trust collapse after top-down pylon decisions. After the Hinkley Point C grid link forced new pylons across the Levels, she now pushes for mandatory undergrounding tests and bill rebates for host villages. She will back a 2050 net zero target only if grid upgrades have a legal duty to test undergrounding in sensitive landscapes and guarantee automatic bill rebates for directly affected parishes. She wants Ofgem to mandate whole-life cost appraisals that factor in visual amenity and biodiversity impacts so undergrounding in sensitive landscapes isn’t ruled out on upfront cost alone. During the Hinkley link, pylon works blocked our lanes for months and hit village B&B income, so I now insist on automatic bill rebates for affected parishes.

This person is a manager in airline operations at Heathrow in his late 30s who wants the transition to prioritize a UK sustainable aviation fuel mandate with price support (such as contracts for difference), airspace modernization and efficiency standards, and coordination with CORSIA rather than unilateral tax hikes that could shift traffic, because he must keep routes viable while decarbonising. After running a trial that cut fuel burn by about 4% using continuous descent and optimized routing, he became convinced airspace modernization should come before new taxes. He's currently negotiating a five-year SAF offtake but says he can't sign without a UK contracts-for-difference backstop to close the price gap and avoid cutting marginal routes. He’s costed the SAF offtake and says that without a CfD the £300–£400 per tonne premium would force him to drop thin domestic rotations to keep long‑haul viable. I need any UK SAF CfD to be book-and-claim compatible and aligned with CORSIA/UK ETS so we can avoid double charges and keep thin regional routes viable.

This person is a rail transport planner and passenger advocate in Greater Manchester in her mid-30s who argues the policy should fund a rolling electrification program, restore and expand canceled HS2 and Northern Powerhouse Rail capacity, integrate fares and ticketing, and rebalance taxes to discourage short‑haul flights where rail is competitive, because modal shift is the fastest way to cut transport emissions. Working on the TransPennine Route Upgrade through Manchester, I saw stop‑start funding lock in diesel operations and suppress mode shift for years. When a funding pause forced weeks of rail‑replacement buses on my TransPennine commute, I watched colleagues revert to cars, cementing my push for continuous electrification. A past funding pause cost my team half our electrification engineers, who left for Scotland’s rolling program and never returned. Restoring HS2 to Manchester matters most to me because the released capacity at Piccadilly is what makes our TransPennine electrics truly turn‑up‑and‑go.

This person is a 42-year-old offshore wind project finance director in Aberdeen who wants the UK to hit net zero by accelerating delivery: statutory 12-month offshore consent timelines, coordinated offshore transmission (not radial spaghetti), anticipatory grid investment, and predictable Contracts for Difference with supply-chain sustainability criteria. They push for faster marine spatial planning that balances habitats protection with clear leasing maps, port upgrade funds for nacelle and blade manufacturing, and a stable carbon price floor to underpin investment. They care because they have seen deals stall over grid connection queues and planning uncertainty that drive up consumer costs and risk the UK losing projects to the EU. If the carbon price floor or CfD terms stay unpredictable, my investment committee will shift our next £2bn of offshore capital to Dutch and German auctions with bankable timelines. After CfD AR5 produced no offshore awards, we froze FID on an 800 MW Moray Firth project and paused 100 Aberdeen hires until indexation and a stable UK ETS price floor are in place. If offshore consents aren’t capped at 12 months, our EPC and turbine options expire, triggering £10m+ in delay penalties and re-pricing. After AR5, our investment committee raised our UK offshore hurdle rate by 150 bps until CfDs have dependable CPI indexation and a stable UK ETS carbon price floor.

This person is a 55-year-old trawler captain out of Grimsby who supports net zero but demands marine policies that do not crush fishing livelihoods: binding requirements for fishing corridors through wind arrays, cumulative impact assessments across projects (not site-by-site), and a statutory compensation and gear-adaptation fund paid from offshore wind revenues. They want seasonal rather than permanent closures where possible, co-designed monitoring with fishermen on board, and rules to site cables away from key grounds. They care because their catches and safety have already been affected by poorly marked infrastructure and piecemeal planning. Last year he lost a week’s earnings when a poorly marked export cable fouled his trawl gear, cementing his call for cable routes off key grounds and automatic compensation. Because he runs a 24m twin-rig trawler, he wants corridor widths based on gear spread and safe turning radii, not turbine spacing alone. He notes that detours around multiple arrays add 6–8 hours of steaming and about £700 in fuel to a typical four-day trip, so cumulative impact assessments must count transit time, not just lost ground. I’ve priced semi-pelagic doors and fuel-flow meters that would cut my fuel burn about 12%, but without a wind-funded gear-upgrade grant I can’t justify the £55k outlay.

This person is a 50-year-old gas boiler installer who runs a six-person SME in Bradford and wants a practical, staged heat transition: a clear end date for new gas-only boilers paired with a guaranteed five-year training voucher scheme, recognition of hybrid heat pumps for hard-to-insulate homes, and simplified certification (reduce MCS paperwork) without compromising quality. They argue for rebalancing levies off electricity so heat pumps are cheaper to run, EPC reform to reflect low-temperature systems, and grant eligibility for small landlords and social housing so their order book does not vanish overnight. They care because rushed bans and cheap unqualified competitors could sink their family business. After the Green Homes Grant collapsed, I was left with sunk training costs and no pipeline, so I won’t retrain all six staff without a guaranteed five-year voucher scheme. Around half our jobs are in hard-to-insulate Bradford terraces, so recognising hybrid heat pumps would let us decarbonise without losing clients to impossible retrofit costs. Without shifting levies off electricity, my heat pump quotes look £300–£500 a year worse on running costs, and customers walk. If ministers pull forward a 2030 boiler ban without funded retraining, I'd have to lay off two fitters and stop taking on apprentices.

This person is a 33-year-old product manager at a UK heat pump manufacturer in Bristol who wants firm signals: a 2033 end date for gas boiler sales, heat-pump-ready standards in all new builds by 2026, scaled Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants with top-ups for off-gas rural homes, and streamlined permitted development for external units. They push for electricity/gas price rebalancing by shifting policy costs to general taxation, mass procurement to cut unit costs, and local training academies to expand the qualified workforce. They care because predictable demand lets them invest in UK assembly lines and bring down costs for households. After losing a 500-home housing association retrofit because planning dragged on for outdoor units, I'm now most focused on streamlined permitted development. If permitted development for outdoor units were truly streamlined to 28 days, we'd green-light a second assembly shift in Bristol immediately. That planning collapse forced me to cancel 12 installer apprenticeships, so a real 28-day deemed-consent for outdoor units is the change I’m fighting for. We're currently sitting on £250,000 of finished outdoor units waiting on overdue planning approvals, so a real 28-day deemed consent would free the cashflow to reinstate our 12 cancelled apprenticeships.

This person is a 29-year-old low-income renter in Tottenham on a prepayment meter who supports net zero but demands it not be funded regressively: move policy levies from electricity bills to progressive taxation, cap standing charges, and ban forced prepayment switches. They want minimum energy efficiency standards to EPC C for rentals with deadlines that trigger landlord grants, paired with rent-rise caps to prevent displacement. They advocate area-based retrofits with trusted local installers, Heat Network tariff protections, and a one-stop shop to actually navigate grants. They care because their cold, damp flat is expensive to heat and past schemes never reached them. Last winter I had to self-disconnect several times because the standing charge kept draining my prepay credit even when I wasn’t using any energy. I even got a bailiff letter for a forced prepay switch last winter, so a real ban on warrants—not just a pause—is a red line for me. Three installers ghosted me when I tried to get quotes, so area-based retrofits with trusted local firms feel like the only way I’d actually get work done. I’m on Economy 7 in an all‑electric flat with old storage heaters, so green levies on electricity and high standing charges hit me hardest.

This person is a 47-year-old local authority housing decarbonisation officer in Greater Manchester who wants multi-year, devolved funding and realistic delivery rules: 10-year capital settlements for area-based retrofits, flexibility in PAS 2035 for solid-wall terraces, and data sharing from energy suppliers to target fuel poverty. They ask for enforcement teeth on landlord standards, a property MOT to track upgrades at sale or let, and permitted development for external wall insulation and air-source heat pumps. They care because stop-start grants and rigid rules strand projects mid-street and waste scarce council capacity. Last year we pulled scaffolding off a row of solid-wall terraces in Oldham mid-EWI when the grant window closed, and those residents still call me weekly. After losing three trained retrofit coordinators to the private sector during the last funding gap, I’m convinced the 2050 goal only works if it comes with predictable, devolved budgets. With 10-year devolved budgets I can lock in local supply chains for whole-street EWI and heat pumps; with annual pots we just churn staff and bids. PAS 2035 needs a solid-wall pathway that permits breathable lime render and brick slips on pre-1919 terraces without failing audits or blowing budgets.

This person is a 44-year-old union convenor at the Port Talbot steelworks who backs net zero if it protects good jobs: a bespoke contract-for-difference for low-carbon steel, a UK carbon border adjustment to stop dirty imports, and funded pilots for hydrogen DRI or EAF with guaranteed affordable power. They want just transition deals covering retraining, wage protection during retooling, and worker voice in tech choices, plus green public procurement for low-embodied-carbon steel in HS2 and housing. They care because their members cannot gamble mortgages on policy vagueness or a sudden furnace shutdown. After negotiating through a 2020 furnace outage that wiped out overtime for a month, he won't support any decarbonisation retooling without paid retraining and guaranteed wage floors. We need a UK carbon border adjustment in force before ETS free allowances end, or our order book and overtime will vanish. If the UK CBAM lags the EU's 2026 start, imported hot-rolled coil will undercut us overnight and weekend overtime will be the first to go. I’ve got 23 apprentices in my cohort and I need assurances their NVQs map to the new kit, not dead‑end qualifications.

This person is a 26-year-old climate justice and circular economy researcher in London who opposes locking in fossil infrastructure and wants demand-side policy first: mandatory product standards and material passports to cut steel use, recycled-content requirements, and green public procurement to drive scrap-based EAF over CCS on blast furnaces. They support a CBAM tied to climate finance for developing countries, no public subsidies for fossil CCS outside hard-to-abate residuals, and timelines to halve industrial emissions by 2035. They care because they see CCS overuse as delaying real change and shifting costs to future taxpayers. In a GLA retrofit pilot I worked on, recycled-content procurement shifted steel orders to UK EAF mills within months, proving demand-side policy moves faster than CCS. I’d be directly affected if the net-zero plan mandates material passports across public projects, since I implement those pilots with London councils. If the net-zero plan backs CCS subsidies over procurement standards, my councils will shelve our passport rollouts for lack of demand signals. I’m pushing for a 40% recycled-steel requirement in public projects by 2028 because it would trigger our material passport rollout across five London councils.

This person is a 61-year-old Welsh hill farmer in Powys who accepts net zero but insists on viable land policies: ELMS payments that reward hedgerows, peat protection, and agroforestry without blanket conifer planting on productive pasture; recognition of stable methane (GWP*) to set fair livestock targets; grants for slurry covers and methane inhibitors; and on-farm solar and small anaerobic digestion with quick grid connections. They want border standards so food imports meet UK environmental rules. They care because one-size-fits-all tree targets threaten their family farm and Welsh-speaking community. When the hill farm next door was sold for carbon-offset sitka spruce, our mart lost trade and the Welsh-medium primary lost two families. I’ve costed a 40 kW roof solar array and a small slurry-fed digester, but the grid operator quoted a three-year wait and £80,000 to connect. If targets ignore GWP* and treat my flock’s steady methane as new emissions, I’ll have to cut breeding ewes just to comply. I fenced off a boggy acre of peat last year and took the hit on summer grazing, so ELMS paying properly for peat and hedges is make-or-break for us.

This person is a 40-year-old director of a rewilding NGO in the Scottish Highlands who wants nature-based solutions embedded in net zero: legally binding nature targets alongside the carbon budget, large-scale peatland and saltmarsh restoration with rigorous MRV, and public-private blended finance with strong additionality tests for carbon credits. They urge limits on bioenergy with carbon capture to true residues, biodiversity net gain extended offshore, and long-term tenure security for landscape projects plus community benefit funds. They care because restoring ecosystems can sequester carbon and cut flood risk more cheaply than engineered fixes if policy stops subsidising perverse land uses. Their NGO has a shovel-ready 10,000-hectare peatland and saltmarsh restoration pipeline that will stall without 30-year tenure security and high-integrity carbon credit rules. Our last £5m blended-finance deal collapsed because two estates could only offer 12-year leases, so without 30-year tenure our 10,000-hectare pipeline stays unfunded. After watching our pilot saltmarsh at Findhorn blunt the 2021 storm surge that overtopped nearby hard defences, I’m determined that legally binding nature targets are written into the 2050 plan. Losing that £5m deal meant laying off our seasonal restoration crews last winter, so I need the 2050 plan to lock in 30-year tenure and high-integrity credits to keep people working.
